title: Ποιμὴν καὶ κύων ⟨τὰ πρόβατα σαίνων⟩
titleEn: The Shepherd and the Dog that Fawned on the Sheep
part: The Shepherd and the Dog that Fawned on the Sheep (Chambry 312)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 312. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ποιμὴν ἔχων κύνα παμμεγέθη τούτῳ εἰώθει τὰ ἔμβρυα καὶ τὰ ἀποθνήσκοντα τῶν προβάτων παραβάλλειν.
sentences.tr: Poimēn echōn kyna pammegethē toutōi eiōthei ta embrya kai ta apothnēskonta tōn probatōn paraballein.
sentences.l: A shepherd, having a huge dog, was accustomed to throw down to it the unborn young and the dying among his sheep.
sentences.i: A shepherd who kept a huge dog was in the habit of throwing it the sheep's unborn young and any of them that were dying.
sentences.n: εἰώθει is the pluperfect of ἔθω carrying plain imperfect force — 'he was in the habit'. ἔμβρυον is the young still in the womb, so what goes to the dog is what is lost before birth, together with the beasts already dying; the word is also used of newborn lambs, and either sense will stand here. παραβάλλω is the regular word for throwing food down beside an animal. Chambry supplies the descriptive half of the title, ⟨τὰ πρόβατα σαίνων⟩, in the angle brackets that mark words he adds.

sentences.t: Καὶ δή ποτε εἰσελθούσης τῆς ποίμνης, ὁ ποιμὴν θεασάμενος τὸν κύνα προσιόντα τοῖς προβάτοις καὶ σαίνοντα αὐτὰ εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’, ὦ οὗτος, ὃ θέλεις σὺ τούτοις ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ κεφαλῇ γένοιτο. »
sentences.tr: Kai dē pote eiselthousēs tēs poimnēs, ho poimēn theasamenos ton kyna prosionta tois probatois kai sainonta auta eipen· « All’, ō houtos, ho theleis sy toutois epi tēi sēi kephalēi genoito. »
sentences.l: And indeed once, the flock having come in, the shepherd, having seen the dog going up to the sheep and fawning on them, said: « Well now, you there — what you wish for these, may it come upon your own head. »
sentences.i: And one day, when the flock had come in, the shepherd saw the dog go up to the sheep and fawn on them, and said: « You there — whatever you have in mind for these, may it fall on your own head. »
sentences.n: ὦ οὗτος is the abrupt Greek 'you there', a shout rather than a courtesy. ὃ θέλεις σὺ τούτοις leaves the verb unsaid — 'what you want for them', which is their death; the shepherd reads the tail-wagging as appetite. γένοιτο is the optative of wish, the standard shape of a curse, and ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ κεφαλῇ, 'on your own head', is as idiomatic in Greek as in English.

sentences.t: Πρὸς ἄνδρα κόλακα ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος.
sentences.tr: Pros andra kolaka ho logos eukairos.
sentences.l: Against a flattering man the story is well-timed.
sentences.i: The story is well aimed at the flatterer.
sentences.n: κόλαξ is the flatterer who attaches himself for what he can get out of it — the moral reads the dog's fawning as exactly that, and πρός with the accusative in this formula is hostile.
